stories.headline: Inside the stunning 72-hour Lakers sale -- and the uncertainty that still looms
stories.summary: Three days of secret talks resulted in Mark Walter flipping the Lakers -- and reignited yet another round of bickering among the six Buss siblings.
stories.body:
BOB IGER WAS on his 213-foot sailing superyacht on Aug. 12, winding down a monthlong vacation in Europe following a historic, two-decade run as CEO of Disney.

The biggest event of the day was supposed to be the first total solar eclipse over the continent in more than a century.

Millions of tourists, including Iger, had booked vacations along the eclipse's path from Greenland to Southern Spain during the syzygy -- a word derived from Ancient Greek for "yoked together" -- which describes a rare astronomical event in which three or more celestial bodies align in a straight line.

During a solar eclipse, the moon sits exactly between the sun and Earth, casting its shadow onto Earth. Some enjoy the rare view -- through special sunglasses.

Others ascribe great meaning and magic to eclipses. As those tourists headed to viewing spots for the solar eclipse across Europe, Iger was in a wholly different syzygy with his longtime friend and business partner Josh Kushner and Los Angeles Lakers owner Mark Walter.

The alignment of three financial heavy hitters was about to turn what should have been a once-in-a-generation event -- last year's record-breaking sale of the Lakers from the Buss family to Walter -- into the NBA's most shocking news -- again.

Instead of getting into position to watch the solar eclipse, Iger was furiously working the phones from Italy to consummate a stunning event of his own -- a $12.5 billion sale of the Lakers seemingly out of nowhere, creating an eclipse unto itself across the worlds of sports and business.

Little did anyone know that these secret, cross-continental talks were about to put the Lakers in significant transition yet again -- with new owners evaluating everything and everyone; squabbling former owners again jostling for power and money; and an overhauled roster finally built in the image of its superstar, Luka Doncic.

Interviews with more than a dozen team insiders, league executives and others with intimate knowledge of the sale reveal how the deal, which was made over a furious 72 hours, upstaged an already-transformative offseason -- and reignited yet another unresolved round of messy public bickering among the six Buss siblings that still hangs uncomfortably over the beginning of this new season.

JUST A YEAR ago, Lakers governor Jeanie Buss had shocked the sports world by negotiating a sale to Walter after 46 years of family ownership. Though that deal was eventually approved by all six siblings, it was not a clean process.

According to several family sources, younger brothers Joey and Jesse Buss -- who, because of a "last-man standing" provision in Dr. Jerry Buss's family trust, were positioned to run the team one day after their older siblings died -- hadn't responded to the vote when the sale was initially announced.

If the family was going to sell, Joey and Jesse wanted to be a part of the process. They had recently pitched to the other siblings a way to sell a minority share -- albeit, sources with knowledge of the discussions said, at a lower valuation than the $10 billion their older sister subsequently agreed to in the deal with Walter. The younger Buss brothers eventually joined their four older siblings in voting for the sale to Walter, but the process created animosity.

Several siblings grumbled that Jeanie had not opened the bidding to outside buyers and had, instead, negotiated directly with Walter, multiple family sources said.

Walter, who already owned 27% of the Lakers, had the right of first refusal on any eventual sale of the Buss family's remaining shares, but how did anyone know how much the team would've fetched without actually putting it on the open market?

The relationship between Jeanie and her siblings disintegrated further when the Lakers, with Jeanie's approval, fired Janie, Joey and Jesse from their respective positions with the franchise within two months of closing on the sale.

All three had expected they'd keep their roles for at least some time while Jeanie was still the controlling owner, multiple family sources said.

The deal with Walter included contractual language to keep Jeanie in charge for the next five seasons but contained no such protections for any other family members.

Janie told ESPN's Baxter Holmes last season that her sister's actions had made her feel disrespected, like a "crumpled-up piece of paper thrown into the trash." She cited the desires of their father, who had purchased the Lakers in 1979 and died in 2013.

"I don't think my dad would be happy with the way things just went down," Janie told Holmes. "Not at all."

There was even more consternation, those sources said, when the Buss family members were suddenly charged more for hospitality and their tickets to Lakers games shortly before the start of the playoffs as part of a larger restructuring of Lakers business practices.

That familial tension simmered throughout last season -- and came to a boil once again this summer.

FOR MUCH OF 2026, Iger and Kushner had been leading a group bidding for the potential Las Vegas NBA expansion franchise, which the NBA initially projected to go for $6 billion-$8 billion, according to industry and ownership sources.

But those bids had blown by that threshold, those sources said, and were approaching the then-record $10 billion valuation of Walter's sale.

Whichever group won the expansion bid would likely then need to spend what multiple sources estimated would be an additional $2 billion -- at least -- to build an arena in Las Vegas.

The Kushner-Iger group had been regarded as one of the favorites to land the team. Iger has had a longtime business relationship with NBA commissioner Adam Silver, from Iger's days negotiating broadcast rights deals for ABC/ESPN with the NBA. In 2020, the two collaborated with the NBPA to create "the bubble" at the Walt Disney Resorts in Orlando, Florida, where the NBA finished its season amid the COVID-19 pandemic. Iger had also been a longtime season-ticket holder of the LA Clippers, although he notably canceled them last season over the team's treatment of Chris Paul, a close friend of Iger's, sources close to him said.

Other finalists for the Las Vegas expansion franchise included groups headed by Walmart heiress Nancy Walton Laurie and her husband Bill Laurie; Las Vegas Golden Knights owner Bill Foley and former Phoenix Suns CEO Jerry Colangelo; and Canadian businessman Steve Apostolopoulos and former Milwaukee Bucks owner Marc Lasry.

As the Aug. 10 deadline for bids approached, Kushner and Iger discussed their options.

Over the past two decades, the 41-year-old Kushner had made a fortune building his venture capital fund, Thrive Capital, with investments in technology companies such as Instagram, Spotify, Twitch, Stripe and OpenAI. This year, Kushner started a new fund, Thrive Eternal, as a hedge against artificial intelligence.

"These are assets with qualities that cannot be replicated by technology," Thrive Eternal says on its website. "Iconic franchises and cultural institutions rooted in tradition, identity, and shared experience. In a world shaped by abundant intelligence where creation scales and distribution fragments, we believe they will matter even more."

An expansion team is not exactly an iconic brand or a legacy franchise. The Lakers, New York Knicks, Chicago Bulls and Boston Celtics are. None of those was known to be for sale, however. The Knicks had just won an NBA title. The Celtics and Lakers had recently been sold to new owners for record amounts. The Bulls were firmly in the hands of the Reinsdorf family, who have not shown any interest in selling.

Still, Kushner and Iger kicked around the idea.

Would any of the owners of those franchises take a phone call or listen to an offer? How much would it take to pique their interest?

It was a bold, risky pivot to even make calls while they were in the throes of the expansion process. If word got out that they were considering moving away from the expansion franchise, would it risk their standing with the NBA?

Whatever they did would need to be quick -- and quiet.

WALTER WAS ON a ranch with spotty cellphone service on Aug. 9, when he got a call from a friend, asking whether he'd consider selling the Lakers, according to three sources with knowledge of his whereabouts and thinking.

The first conversation was short. The Lakers weren't for sale, Walter told his friend, who relayed the message to Kushner and Iger. But the two businessmen had reason to persevere in their efforts.

Two days earlier, on Aug. 7, they had called a well-connected financial industry source who was close enough to Walter to suggest he might be looking to restructure some of his business assets amid federal investigations of alleged fraud within his sprawling $365 billion financial empire, according to multiple sources with knowledge of the conversations.

They figured it was worth dropping a line in the water, baiting the hook at a number that would make him think about it.

The only catch was they needed an answer within 24 hours. There was no time for a long negotiation or intermediaries.

Kushner made the next call to Walter, according to multiple sources with knowledge of the negotiation, and Kushner offered to buy Walter's shares at a $12.5 billion valuation -- a 25% increase in 14 months.

It was the kind of staggering "Godfather offer" Walter had presented to Jeanie Buss when he convinced her to sell him the majority of her family's shares a year earlier.

Walter decided to cut short his weekend trip and get to a place with better cellphone reception. They had his attention. By Monday, he had returned to his estate in White Oak, Florida.

He called his wife, Kimbra, and daughter, Samantha, and asked what they thought of him selling the Lakers.

He outlined the enormous return he'd make at this valuation -- nearly $4 billion because he had bought the first 27% of his Lakers shares at a $5 billion valuation in 2021 -- and the benefits that liquidity could provide him, given the remediation plans he had proposed to state insurance regulators.

Neither his wife nor daughter had an issue with him selling the Lakers, those sources said. They had been involved with the Los Angeles Dodgers for 14 years, but their attachment to the Lakers was still new.

After Walter's family signed off, the circle of people involved in the negotiations widened.

Advisers on both sides were sworn to secrecy. There wasn't time for Kushner and Iger's group to do anything resembling due diligence. They were buying the brand, as is, with as quick a close as you'll ever see in a $12.5 billion deal.

By the evening of Aug. 11 -- 72 hours after the idea had first been presented to him -- Walter had come to an agreement with Iger and Kushner.

JEANIE BUSS LEARNED of Walter's agreement to sell his shares of the Lakers hours before ESPN reported the news on the morning of Aug. 12, according to multiple sources with knowledge of their conversations.

She was stunned, according to sources close to her.

This was not what she had planned for or expected when she reached out to Walter in 2021 to suggest he purchase Philip Anschutz's shares to become the largest minority shareholder in the franchise, and with it, hold the first right of refusal to buy the Buss family's shares for a controlling interest in the team.

Walter and Buss had built a relationship over many years before he expressed an interest in buying into the Lakers.

Over the decade he owned the Dodgers, Walter had actively built bridges between L.A.'s premier baseball team and its basketball team. Lakers legend Magic Johnson was part of Walter's ownership group. Dodgers players were often invited to and hosted at Lakers games, and vice versa. Walter often attended games with Buss, while Buss attended Dodgers games with Walter.

At the time he bought Anschutz's shares, only people very close to the situation understood why it was so significant. Buss had essentially chosen Walter as her successor. Whenever she was ready to sell her family's controlling shares, he would have the inside track to buy them.

Buss chose Walter, multiple sources close to her said, because of how he owned and operated the Dodgers and the positive reviews he had gotten from associates of hers, including Johnson, tennis legend Billie Jean King and longtime Dodgers executive Lon Rosen. She had compared him to her father, Dr. Jerry Buss, for his commitment to winning publicly and privately over the years.

To those close to the situation, the question wasn't whether the Buss family would eventually sell to Walter but when. Older brothers Johnny and Jim had wanted to sell the team for years.

Jeanie, her sister Janie and younger brothers Joey and Jesse still had roles with the team and wanted to stay on longer.

In 2025, Walter came up with an offer he thought would make everyone happy: a $10 billion valuation -- generating approximately $800 million for each sibling -- and an agreement for Jeanie to stay on as controlling owner for five years, codified in writing as part of the agreement.

"Over the past decade, I have come to know Mark well -- first as a businessman, then as a friend and now as a colleague," Jeanie Buss said in a statement after the sale. "He has demonstrated time and time again his commitment to bringing championships to Los Angeles, and, on behalf of Lakers fans everywhere, I am beyond excited about what our future has in store."

Buss even showed that paperwork to Doncic and his team, his manager Lara Beth Seager said, to reassure them that she would still have final say over his basketball future.

Doncic had learned the hard way how an ownership change could affect him after his shocking trade from the Dallas Mavericks to the Lakers in February 2025.

Former Mavericks owner Mark Cuban also thought he'd be allowed to stay on as head of basketball operations when he sold his controlling stake to the Adelson family in 2023. Cuban swore to Doncic that he wanted him to be a Maverick for life, but wasn't involved or included in the trade discussions that sent Doncic to L.A.

This time, it was Jeanie who would learn the hard way -- that whatever relationship she had built with Walter and others would be superseded by the harsh realities of the modern business world.

DESPITE THAT RELATIONSHIP, the man Jeanie chose as the next steward of the Lakers was not the rock-solid titan of the financial industry he appeared to be.

Walter, the public would soon learn, was under multiple federal criminal investigations before his purchase of the Lakers became official at the end of October. According to the Wall Street Journal, the FBI on Sept. 18, 2025, conducted a raid of a private plane at Chicago's Midway Airport, where Walter had been traveling, and seized a laptop and mobile phone.

Just 10 months later, Walter flipped the Lakers like a cold asset, not a crown-jewel, generational investment.

After five decades of family ownership, Jeanie had relinquished control of her family's most prized possession to someone who had treated it no differently than any other line item in his massive portfolio.

"I mean, he made $2.5 billion in 10 months by flipping the Lakers like a spec house," one family confidant said. "But that wasn't supposed to be the deal. Jeanie picked him because he was going to own it like he's owned the Dodgers."

Walter has not spoken publicly about the sale outside of an initial statement he released to ESPN.

In late August, his company, The Walter Group, issued a statement asserting it had been subjected to "multipronged attacks" from "unnamed sources with self-serving interests."

The statement said that TWG and its Group 1001 insurance companies had presented a plan to state insurance regulators to address regulatory concerns over a percentage of affiliated transactions it had misreported in its filings. TWG explained that the affiliated transactions in question are "common across the insurance industry" and "suggestions that TWG is looting insurers is defamatory and false."

Investigators are still looking into the company's dealings as it makes changes in the way it operates. TWG Global announced in late August that it had swapped out $6.5 billion of its assets to replace the type of affiliated loans regulators had taken issue with. The dual sales of the Lakers and Walter's minority 12.8% stake in Premier League club Chelsea have raised additional capital, while also leading to an assortment of buyers inquiring about the availability of the Dodgers and Los Angeles Sparks.

The company has emphatically denied that it is looking to sell its sports assets at "fire sale" prices to raise capital for its insurance operations. The sales of the Lakers and Chelsea came in at significant valuations -- a record in the case of the Lakers. However, sources with knowledge of the situation confirm a Bloomberg report that acknowledged there have been early-stage discussions about the Sparks at what would be a similarly massive valuation, estimated at $700 million.

Inquiries for the Dodgers have thus far been rebuffed, those sources said.

IGER LANDED BACK home in Los Angeles a few days after the sale agreement was reached. The first visitor he entertained at his house was Jeanie Buss, according to multiple sources with knowledge of the meeting.

He had given public comments to the California Post immediately after news of the sale broke that the new ownership group intended to honor the agreement Buss had with Walter to stay on as controlling owner, but added, "if something changes, then it changes."

Despite the public hedge, Iger reaffirmed his commitment to Jeanie to maintain a role after the sale closes when they met, those sources said. They have stayed in regular contact since then.

Whether she'll be able to do so -- and what that role ultimately is -- depends on how the latest round of family discord is resolved.

By the time Walter decided to sell his stake in the Lakers in mid-August, family sources said there had already been renewed calls among the siblings to sell the remaining 17.8% of the team that the family owned.

The Lakers had fired four of her siblings already. Jim Buss, who was fired in 2017, noted to the group that there was little justification for keeping the family's remaining shares, other than nostalgia and Jeanie keeping her controlling-ownership power for four additional years, according to multiple family sources. He circulated a proposal he hoped would satisfy all parties.

On the night of Aug. 10, two days before the sale, Lakers vice president of finance Joe McCormack called for a meeting of the Buss siblings to discuss a dissolution of the family trust and seek approval to lock down all family shares for four years under a new trust, according to ESPN's Dave McMenamin.

When the family discussed McCormack's proposal on Aug. 11, no mention was made of Walter's impending sale to Kushner and Iger. The family woke up to the news of the massive sale the following morning like everyone else.

On Aug. 17, ESPN's Shams Charania reported that Johnny, Jim, Janie, Joey and Jesse Buss had voted to sell the remaining family shares to Iger and Kushner, using "go-along" rights they had been given as part of the sale to Walter. (Technically, those rights can be only invoked once Walter officially notifies the family that he has signed a deal to sell, which hasn't happened yet.)

Jeanie was the only family member who did not vote to sell. In fact, she did not even respond to the vote that had been called a week earlier.

Later that day, her lawyer, Adam Streisand, sent a letter to the five siblings, challenging the legality of their vote based on a 2017 court order that required the two co-trustees, Janie and Joey, to always vote to ensure she remained the controlling owner of the team.

The siblings immediately responded to Streisand's initial letter with a statement of their own, reaffirming their desire to sell. They contended they needed only a majority (four of six votes and two of three co-trustees) to enact that go-along provision, according to sources with knowledge of the siblings' position.

Jeanie currently controls the Buss family trust, which owns 17.8% of the Lakers. NBA rules mandate that a controlling owner must own at least 15% of the team. An alternate governor must own at least 5%.

Still, multiple family sources said there have been settlement talks between the two sides over the past two months.

Each sibling stands to make an additional $371 million if the family sells the entirety of its shares via the go-along provision.

The siblings could also try to find a buyer at a higher valuation, a possibility fueled by a pitch, which The Wall Street Journal obtained, to Thrive Eternal investors in which the company projected the Lakers valuation to be at least $30 billion within a decade.

The dispute spilled back into the public on Oct. 7, when the five siblings formally filed a response to Jeanie's suit.

"Jimmy, Johnny, Janie, Joey and Jesse Buss, the five of six siblings who voted to sell the Trust's shares in the Lakers, today filed their formal opposition, demonstrating that Jeanie Buss's petition is legally and factually baseless," the siblings said in a statement issued to ESPN.

"While discussions among the siblings continue, their focus remains on facilitating the proposed transaction and the [Buss family] trust's participation in it, while ensuring that all beneficiaries, including Jeanie, are treated equally."

Nine days later, the five siblings submitted, on behalf of Joey and Janie, an additional filing, this one challenging Jeanie and her previous petition that seeks to remove them as co-trustees and void the siblings' 5-1 vote to sell the family's remaining stake in the team.

Through it all, the foundation of the dispute remains the same: whether the five siblings can sell their share of the team without Jeanie's approval.

A court date is set for Dec. 8 if no settlement is reached.

DONCIC WAS THE only person outside of the small circle of people close to Walter, Kushner and Iger who had any inkling how the sports world was about to dramatically change before Aug. 12.

The last time he had gotten a text from Seager, his longtime manager, at an odd hour was in February 2025, when she reached him after midnight and told him he had been traded to the Lakers.

This time, she had gotten a tip well after midnight at her home in Dallas that something big might be happening again. She texted Doncic, who was just waking up in Slovenia, alerting him to the possibility.

All summer, they had been planning a five-day team bonding retreat in Doncic's home country for his new Lakers teammates. On the first night, they'd all eat at his favorite restaurant, Cubo, in his hometown of Ljubljana.

Then, they'd play golf some 40 miles north on the perfectly manicured grounds of Royal Bled, sitting in a valley beneath the tree-lined peaks of the Alps. Another day was built around rowing lessons on Lake Bled, taught by Slovenian Olympian Jani Klemencic. Three high-speed boats, 15 Lakers, learning to row together.

Then, in one early-morning text, all those plans seemed secondary.

It was a stunning turn with no forewarning. Just a week earlier, Seager had met Jeanie and Rosen for dinner. Nothing had seemed amiss. At that point, Kushner had yet to engage Walter about the possibility of buying the Lakers.

Doncic had developed a good relationship with Walter and Jeanie Buss in the 18 months since he had come to Los Angeles, meeting and texting with both of them regularly. Walter even took him and a group of teammates to a Backstreet Boys concert at The Sphere in Las Vegas last summer, after Doncic agreed to a three-year, $165 million contract extension with the Lakers.

If the sale goes through and Kushner and Iger are approved by the NBA, and that is expected to happen by the end of the year or early next year, according to multiple sources close to the sale process, they'd be his fifth team owners across two franchises in the past three years.

By the time Seager called Doncic to tell him the deal was done, he had already processed the initial shock.

"There's not much that can shock me anymore," Doncic told her.

The next day, as he congratulated the new owners, he acknowledged the seismic move and posted on X:

"I've gotten used to big changes over these last few years."

stories.headline: AFL 2027 fixture: Five must-watch games in the first month
stories.summary: The 2027 AFL fixture has been released. So, to whet your appetite for the upcoming season, we've picked out the five must-watch games from the opening month.
stories.body:
The 2027 AFL fixture has been released. So, to whet your appetite for the upcoming season, we've picked out the five must-watch games from the opening month of action.

Get the popcorn ready and get set to enjoy these absolute belters in the new year.

5. Port Adelaide vs. Western Bulldogs - Round 4, Adelaide Oval, Sunday, April 8, 7:40pm (AEDT)
Make no mistake, when Zak Butters returns to Adelaide Oval to face his old mob for the first time since departing, it's going to be incredibly spicy.

In a move that shocked absolutely nobody, Butters left Port Adelaide during the 2026 trade period, inking a long-term deal with the Western Bulldogs. It's a brutal blow for the Power, and his ex-teammates will be sure to give him a hard time when they share the field in Round 4. You just know it's going to be on for young and old!

The AFL also made the move to schedule this blockbuster game as the closer to next year's Gather Round. It means far more bodies will be in Adelaide that weekend and a greater number of eyeballs on the clash.

4. Hawthorn vs. Geelong - Round 2, MCG, Monday, March 29, 3:15pm (AEDT)
The traditional Easter Monday clash between the Hawks and Cats is always on our shortlist of early season must-watch games, and next year will be no exception.

Both of these clubs are in the premiership window. Both clubs have added high-profile players this offseason. Both clubs have fanbases that bring an electric energy to Easter Monday at the MCG.

This one is also set to be a fascinating coaching battle between Chris Scott and Sam Mitchell, two of the game's best tacticians, who will go head-to-head just as much as the players on the field.

3. Fremantle vs. Western Bulldogs - Round 1, Optus Stadium, Thursday, March 18, 8:10pm (AEDT)
This Round 1 game in the west is simply oozing with intrigue.

Of course, the question on everyone's mind is how the Dockers back up after having this year's premiership ripped away from them in harrowing circumstances. Does it galvanise the club? Will we see 'Wharfie Time'? Surely not!

For the Bulldogs, they landed the biggest fish of the off-season in superstar midfielder Zak Butters. This will be the first opportunity to watch him play in his new colours, lining up in the middle alongside skipper Marcus Bontempelli and Ed Richards.

2. Brisbane vs. Collingwood - Round 2, Gabba, Thursday, March 25, 7:50pm (AEDT)
Reigning premier Brisbane will unfurl its latest flag in Round 2 when it hosts Collingwood in its first home game of the season, a clash that has blockbuster written all over it.

The Lions are looking to become just the second team ever to win four consecutive flags (joining, you guessed it, Collingwood from 1927 to 1930) but will be doing it without superstar midfielder Lachie Neale. The two-time Brownlow medallist departed for the Magpies this offseason, making this early season contest between the two clubs extra intriguing.

Plus, any opportunity to watch current Brownlow medallist Nick Daicos play footy is reason in itself to tune in!

1. Hawthorn vs. Brisbane - Round 1, MCG, Friday, March 19, 7:40pm (AEDT)
Thankfully we don't have to wait long for the Hawks and Lions -- quite possibly the competition's two best teams -- to square off in 2027. And if this game delivers even 70% of what these sides dished up in this year's epic preliminary final, then we're in for an absolute treat!

Many have labelled Brisbane's thrilling win over Hawthorn this past September as the greatest game of footy played this century. That in itself should be enough of a reason for their next clash to simply be must-watch.

There will be extra intrigue with both teams given this clash falls in Round 1. For the Lions, they will be looking to navigate life without both superstar midfielder Lachie Neale and master coach Chris Fagan, while the Hawks will be attempting to integrate recruits Zach Merrett and Ben King into their line-up.

stories.headline: It's still the age of Volkanovski in MMA pound-for-pound rankings
stories.summary: At age 38, UFC featherweight champion makes big jump in ESPN's P4P top 10.
stories.body:
Alexander Volkanovski made a bold statement at UFC 333 that, even at age 38, he isn't ready to surrender his place among the greatest in MMA. The ESPN pound-for-pound voting panel took note.

On the strength of Volkanovski's second-round knockout of previously undefeated Movsar Evloev on Saturday, the UFC featherweight champion makes a big jump in the latest men's rankings. Volkanovski is No. 2, after entering the weekend five positions lower.

Volkanovski was so impressive that he outshined the co-main event performance of Petr Yan, who defended the men's bantamweight title by beating former champion Merab Dvalishvili. Yan drops one spot to No. 3, the position Dvalishvili used to occupy. Dvalishvili is now tied for eighth after his second straight loss to Yan in their fiery trilogy.

The other significant change near the top of the rankings is the disappearance of Tom Aspinall. The former UFC heavyweight champion is still healing from eye injuries suffered in a no-contest against Ciryl Gane in October 2025. Because Aspinall has not fought in over a year, he is ineligible for the rankings.

For the ESPN divisional MMA rankings, click here.

Note: Results are current; rankings are as of Oct. 28. To be eligible for the rankings, a fighter must have competed over the past 12 months or must have an upcoming fight booked. Fighters who have been dropped for inactivity can be reinstated only after they compete.

Men's pound-for-pound rankings

1. Islam Makhachev

UFC welterweight champion

Record: 29-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Ian Machado Garry, Aug. 15

Next: TBA

Makhachev vacated the UFC lightweight championship to go for a second title at welterweight. By winning that belt last November with a thrashing of Jack Della Maddalena, Makhachev staked his place among MMA's greatest -- not just in today's sport but of all time. His win over Machado Garry at UFC 330 was his 17th straight, breaking the UFC record for consecutive wins. Makhachev is piling up unprecedented achievements.

2. Alexander Volkanovski

UFC featherweight champion

Previous ranking: 7

Record: 29-4

Last: W (TKO2) vs. Movsar Evloev, Oct. 24

Next: TBA

It felt as if the sport had started to write Volkanovski's eulogy following his knockout loss to Ilia Topuria in February 2024. Volkanovski noticed and made a point of proving to everyone he still has plenty left by recapturing the featherweight belt at UFC 314, the first of two consecutive wins over Lopes. His age (38) will likely continue to be a prefight topic, which is fine because Volkanovski enjoys proving people wrong. He did just that by handing Evloev his first loss at UFC 333.

3. Petr Yan

UFC bantamweight champion

Previous ranking: 2

Record: 21-5

Last: W (UD) vs. Merab Dvalishvili, Oct. 24

Next: TBA

What a return to the top it's been for Yan. He began his career with 15 consecutive wins before going on a 1-4 run from 2021 to 2023. That almost doesn't feel real now, after watching him reclaim his throne against Dvalishvili, who once handed him the worst loss of his career, then completing his trilogy with Dvalishvili with a successful title defense. Yan took a major detour, but this was the destination we felt he was capable of before the skid. He once again looks like one of the best fighters on the planet.

4. Ilia Topuria

UFC lightweight

Previous ranking: 6

Record: 17-1

Last: L (TKO4) vs. Justin Gaethje, June 14

Next: TBA

Topuria was an undefeated two-division champion when he ran into Gaethje at UFC Freedom 250 and was brutalized in a stoppage loss. How will that affect the immediate future of Topuria? His knockout wins over two of the greatest featherweights, Alexander Volkanovski and Max Holloway, gave him an intimidating aura. Can the former champion get that back?

5. Justin Gaethje

UFC lightweight champion

Previous ranking: Tied for 4

Record: 28-5

Last: W (TKO4) vs. Ilia Topuria, June 14

Next: TBA

Gaethje has spent his 15-year career thrilling MMA fans, but before the title bout on the White House lawn, all he had to show for it -- aside from 15 bonus checks in 15 UFC appearances -- were two missed opportunities to be an undisputed champion. His fourth-round TKO of Topuria got Gaethje over the hump. It was a resilient performance in a back-and-forth battle that is a prime candidate for fight of the year. More important for Gaethje: At age 37, he is finally sitting at the top of the mountain.

6. Joshua Van

UFC flyweight champion

Previous ranking: 8

Record: 18-2

Last: W (UD) vs. Alexandre Pantoja, Sept. 19

Next: Jan. 30 vs. Manel Kape

Van has been champion since December, but until UFC 331, there were doubters. Van had been handed the belt by default, when his challenge for the title was waved off after 26 seconds because Pantoja dislocated his left elbow. Van went on to defend the title against Tatsuro Taira in May, then faced Pantoja in a rematch at UFC 331. Van produced a clear victory -- his eighth win in a row -- to leave no doubt who rules at 125 pounds.

7. Arman Tsarukyan

UFC lightweight

Previous ranking: 10

Record: 24-3

Last: W (KO1) vs. Mauricio Ruffy, Sept. 19

Next: TBA

Tsarukyan is right back in the place he was in January 2025 -- on the cusp of a title fight. He withdrew from a challenge of Islam Makhachev one day before UFC 311 because of a back injury, and later in the year he was passed over twice when the UFC was booking lightweight title bouts. But by knocking out Ruffy with an elbow in the first round at UFC 331, Tsarukyan put himself back at the front of the line.

T-8. Merab Dvalishvili

UFC bantamweight

Previous ranking: 3

Record: 21-6

Last: L (UD) vs. Petr Yan, Oct. 24

Next: TBA

Dvalishvili was on one of the most impressive runs through the UFC's bantamweight division ever. Not only did he defeat Sean O'Malley for the second time in nine months at UFC 316, but he showcased a new part of his game, finishing O'Malley with a guillotine. Starting in August 2022, Dvalishvili beat José Aldo, Yan, Henry Cejudo, O'Malley (twice), Umar Nurmagomedov and Cory Sandhagen. But at UFC 323, in an attempt to become the first champion in UFC history to successfully defend a title four times in a calendar year, Dvalishvili lost a rematch with Yan. Their third meeting at UFC 333 was the most competitive in their trilogy, but Dvalishvili fell short again.

T-8. Ciryl Gane

UFC heavyweight champion

Previous ranking: 9

Record: 14-2, 1 NC

Last: W (TKO2) vs. Alex Pereira, June 14

Next: Nov. 14 vs. Josh Hokit

Gane is unique in that he is the first -- and could very well go down as the only -- heavyweight to face the division's four biggest names in Francis Ngannou, Jon Jones, Tom Aspinall and Pereira. None of those four have fought each other, yet all four have have fought the Frenchman. Gane was 0-2 with a no-contest against that group before he knocked out Pereira in the second round of their interim title fight on the White House lawn. Gane was elevated to undisputed champ after Aspinall, still injured, vacated his title, and the new champ will defend against Hokit at UFC 334.

10. Alex Pereira

UFC heavyweight

Previous ranking: Unranked

Record: 13-4

Last: L (TKO2) vs. Ciryl Gane, June 14

Next: Dec. 12 vs. Sergei Pavlovich

Pereira made a big splash in the MMA after a world championship career in kickboxing. He joined the UFC in 2021 and became a middleweight champion the following year, then moved on to be a two-time light heavyweight titlist before making an unprecedented bid for a belt in a third weight class when he fought Game at UFC Freedom 250 for an interim heavyweight title. Pereira got knocked out in that fight, but now he's back on his feet and in position to reclaim his position when he faces a fellow title contender, Pavlovich, at UFC 335.

Other fighters receiving votes: Alexandre Pantoja and Sean Strickland.

Women's pound-for-pound rankings

1. Valentina Shevchenko

UFC flyweight

Record: 26-4-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Zhang Weili, Nov. 15, 2025

Next: TBA

Shevchenko's dominance came under question in 2022 and 2023, when she went 1-1-1 in a trilogy with Alexa Grasso. Boy, does that feel like a long time ago now. Shevchenko more than reasserted herself as the best flyweight in the world, and then she established herself as the No. 1 woman in the world, period. It wasn't surprising that she beat Zhang, but it was surprising how easy she made it look. Shevchenko is out injured, however, so she has vacated her UFC title, which Natalia Silva captured by beating Wang Cong at UFC 332. When Shevchenko is healed up, she'll be looking to take back the belt.

2. Zhang Weili

UFC flyweight / strawweight

Record: 26-4

Last: L (UD) vs. Valentina Shevchenko, Nov. 15, 2025

Next: TBA

It's hard to move up in weight, especially at the highest level. That sounds like it should be obvious, but Zhang had been dominant at 115 pounds for so long, some of us might have taken for granted how big of a challenge moving to 125 would be. UFC 322 was a bad night for Zhang, but she doesn't have many. And if she decides to stay at flyweight, it certainly seems reasonable to believe she'll fare better in the future.

3. Cris Cyborg

PFL featherweight champion

Record: 30-2, 1 NC

Last: W (UD) vs. Ketlen Vieira, Aug. 22

Next: TBA

It had been a while since Cyborg had fought an elite opponent in MMA until she met Larissa Pacheco in 2024. That was a legitimate matchup -- and many within the industry were predicting Cyborg's downfall. Instead, she took out the PFL's two-weight champion, upending all of Pacheco's momentum. One of the original pioneers of women's MMA is once again a champion after getting her second career submission at PFL Lyon in December. The PFL promoted her fight with Vieira as a retirement bout, but after her win Cyborg did not sound like someone who is done fighting.

4. Natalia Silva

UFC flyweight champion

Record: 21-5-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Wang Cong, Oct. 3

Next: TBA

Silva was looking every bit the part of a future UFC champion following a dominant display against Alexa Grasso at UFC 315 and a victory over Rose Namajunas at UFC 324. And now she has fulfilled that expectation, beating Wang at UFC 332 to win the belt vacated by injured Valentina Shevchenko. Silva's stick-and-move style has frustrated even the highest level of opponent, and she's got youth on her side as she won't turn 30 until 2027.

5. Mackenzie Dern

UFC strawweight champion

Record: 17-5

Last: W (UD) vs. Gillian Robertson, Aug. 15

Next: TBA

Dern's rise to the 115-pound throne was truly a changing of the guard. She is the division's first first-time champion since 2019, because the previous three champs -- Zhang Weili, Carla Esparza and Rose Namajunas -- all were in their second reigns. Dern, nearly a decade into her MMA career after multiple jiu-jitsu world championships, has won four fights in a row, including a dominant performance against a fellow grappling-heavy fighter, Robertson, in her first title defense.

6. Alexa Grasso

UFC flyweight

Record: 18-5-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Manon Fiorot, Sept. 12

Next: TBA

Grasso went nearly three years without winning a fight, but her 2023 win right before the skid was a huge one, a submission of Valentina Shevchenko for the UFC title. What followed were two more fights with Shevchenko -- a draw, then a loss -- and then a loss to Natalia Silva. But she reasserted herself with a finish of Maycee Barber in March, then got the best of Fiorot, a fellow title contender, at Noche UFC to put herself in position for another title shot.

7. Dakota Ditcheva

PFL flyweight

Record: 16-0

Last: W (UD) vs. Denise Kielholtz, July 31

Next: TBA

Not only did Ditcheva win the PFL's flyweight season in 2024, but she did so in spectacular fashion -- a TKO finish over Taila Santos, who once challenged for a UFC title. Ditcheva fought only once in 2025, dominating Sumiko Inaba in the co-main event of the first PFL Champions Series card in Cape Town, South Africa. She then spent over a year on the sideline, healing injuries to both hands, before returning at PFL New York with a dominant win over Kielholtz.

8. Manon Fiorot

UFC flyweight

Record: 13-3

Last: L (UD) vs. Alexa Grasso, Sept. 12

Next: TBA

Fiorot had handled everyone the UFC put in front of her -- except the champion, Valentina Shevchenko, who defeated the Frenchwoman at UFC 315 in May 2025. But then, with another title shot within her grasp, Fiorot ran into Grasso, a former champion, at Noche UFC and lost a competitive fight.

9. Tatiana Suarez

UFC strawweight

Record: 12-1

Last: W (Sub2) vs. Loopy Godínez, April 11

Next: Nov. 7 vs. Virna Jandiroba

UFC strawweight

Last: W (UD) vs. Tabatha Ricci, April 4

Jandiroba fell short in last October's fight with Mackenzie Dern for the vacant title, but she bounced back in April with a victory over Ricci. Up next is a top-10 showdown with Suarez, who also lost a title challenge last year. The winner will be right back in the championship mix.

stories.headline: WNBA's Houston Comets unveil new logos amid trademark filing
stories.summary: On Wednesday, eight trademark applications for logos appeared on the United States Patent and Trademark Office website.
stories.body:
The Houston Comets spent all week teasing a release on social media of something related to the rebirth of the WNBA franchise, which occurred Thursday night when the team revealed its logos.

On Wednesday, eight trademark applications for logos appeared on the United States Patent and Trademark Office website that proved to be a preview of the franchise's new logos.

The applications, filed by WNBA Enterprises LLC, consisted of four logos, each with two separate applications: one for entertainment services and another for sports jerseys and clothing.

The four logos match those revealed by Houston on Thursday. One features a circular emblem with a stylized letter H. A basketball with a comet tail cuts through the letter, and "Houston Comets" is written around the border.

Another logo -- deemed the primary icon -- features the stylized H without the circular border.

The applications also included secondary logos. One shows "Houston" with four stars scattered amid the letters. A basketball with a comet tail goes through part of the T and O.

Another logo features "Comets" in the same font with the stylized basketball going through part of the C and the O.

The logos, which were applied for without a specific color scheme but were revealed in blue and red on Thursday, were first reported by Josh Gerben, a trademark attorney with Gerben IP. Messages left with the Comets, the WNBA and the WNBA's trademark attorney about the logos were not immediately returned to ESPN.

"There was a way for the WNBA to have filed these trademarks where everybody would not have been able to find them before the announcement," Gerben said. "They could have literally filed them offshore."

Gerben said professional sports franchises have started to initially register trademark applications internationally, specifically in Mauritius and Jamaica, to try to prevent any leaks before logo or naming announcements.

It can be difficult for teams, he said, to balance the timing of applications while avoiding someone else trademarking a name or logo first. Gerben said if a franchise or league files internationally first, it then has a six-month window to file in the United States while holding the initial filing date in the foreign country.

It's unclear if the WNBA did that in this case.

The Comets logo has been a trademark question for the WNBA since it awarded the relocation of the Connecticut Sun to Houston. In 2024, a Delaware-based corporation called TSTM Holdings LLC applied for a trademark of "Houston Comets" for a variety of uses, including clothing, gym bags and other items. It is unknown who owns TSTM Holdings. On Thursday morning, however, TSTM Holdings abandoned its application, according to USPTO records.

stories.headline: Cavan Sullivan turned 17 last month, but he's already playing like an MLS MVP
stories.summary: Since MLS resumed after the World Cup, Cavan Sullivan has been the league's best player not named Lionel Messi. Does he deserve some MVP recognition?
stories.body:
Philadelphia Union interim manager Ryan Richter remembers it well.

He was mindful of midfielder Cavan Sullivan's mood earlier this season. Sullivan was finding playing time hard to come by for a side that was struggling mightily. Even as Richter was spending most of his time managing the Union's reserve team, he couldn't help but notice the demeanor of a player he first coached as an 8-year-old.

"He was pissed," Richter said of Sullivan in an interview with ESPN. "He wanted a chance to play."

He eventually got it, and he has been taking out that anger on the rest of MLS ever since.

As Sullivan and the Union head into this weekend's game against FC Cincinnati, the 17-year-old is nursing an ankle injury, but his rise has been the story of the MLS season. His 21 goal contributions have already broken the league record for a teenager, eclipsing the 20 recorded by the New England Revolution's Diego Fagundez in 2013. Ditto for goal contributions by a player younger than 17, with Sullivan -- who turned 17 in late September -- breaking the mark of 10 set by Freddy Adu in 2005.

His success has been accompanied by a feistiness, his brilliance often combined with a snarl. Such success has led to chatter that since the resumption of league play following the FIFA World Cup, Sullivan is the league MVP, non-Lionel Messi division.

There is a case to be made for slotting him in just behind the former Argentina captain given the Union's change in fortunes. Prior to the World Cup break, Philadelphia was dead last in MLS, with just seven points from 15 matches. Since the break, the Union have a league-best 39 points thanks to a 12-3-1 record and clinched a playoff spot on Wednesday. That the run has coincided with Sullivan's ascension is by no means a fluke.

When the subject of Sullivan's MVP candidacy is brought up to Richter, one can almost hear the grimace over the phone. Part of Richter's job description these days is to slow the collective roll surrounding his young star, and he's not about to stop now.

"There's time to look back and reflect on stuff like that after the season," Richter said about the MVP talk. "Forget about all the other outside noise of what could be. Let's have a f---ing great session today."

Numbers have also served to cool the MVP talk. According to TruMedia -- which doesn't count secondary assists to the same degree that MLS does -- Sullivan's 15 goal contributions since the World Cup break has him seventh in the league, behind such luminaries as Orlando City SC's Antoine Griezmann (22) and Messi (19). Sullivan's contributions aren't even the most on his own team, with Milan Iloski (18) leading the way. Other players, such as Cincinnati's Evander and Hany Mukhtar of the Supporters' Shield-winning Nashville SC have been utterly consistent over the course of the campaign.

The MVP moniker also gets thrown around rather casually, and with Messi taking up so much of the league's oxygen, it's an easy label to affix to a player like Sullivan who is enjoying a stellar run of form. In some respects, the chatter doesn't do Sullivan any favors. He's still just a teenager -- albeit an extraordinarily talented one -- and the MVP label doesn't tell the whole story of his season.

Sullivan's production seemingly came out of nowhere. His 14 league appearances prior to this season yielded no goal contributions. He had just five in MLS play in 13 league appearances through the end of May, but he logged just 549 minutes. There certainly wasn't any MVP talk during the first half of 2026.

Yet Sullivan's rise wasn't something that just happened. It was the result of some meticulous planning on the part of the Union from the time they signed Sullivan as a 14-year-old, as well as the player's hard work. Every step, from the academy and through the reserve team to the first team, was carefully choreographed. While it's easy to draw a demarcation line pre- and post-World Cup, there were signs of a breakthrough prior to the pause for the tournament, as Sullivan began to get on the field with more consistency. That extended playing time freed up his mind to begin playing closer to his best.

"In the very beginning of the season, if [Sullivan] got 10 minutes here and there, he would try to fit everything into those 10 minutes, and it's hard to play like that," Richter said. "And then towards the end -- I would say the end of the first half of the season -- when he got some extended runs and a couple starts, then he really showed that he could do something at this level."

When Richter took over after manager Bradley Carnell was fired at the end of May, he decided there was no way he was taking Sullivan out of the lineup.

"The first conversation with [Sullivan] was just that he's going to get the chance now, like a real chance, not just put him in and see how he does," Richter said. "It's, 'Cav, I believe that you are a great player at this level and I believe that you can be. Now you get a real opportunity with coaches who believe that fully, and you've got to take it.'"

Sullivan didn't wait for the regular season to try to repay that faith. His mentality has long been one of his best traits, and he was determined to maximize the time that the World Cup break afforded him. He played a match for Union II against the Ivory Coast prior to the World Cup, a period when most of the roster was on vacation. He trained with his brother, Quinn Sullivan, and his father Brendan, a former pro player, to maintain his fitness. He then played in four friendlies against MLS opposition, and impressed every time.

"That was an important period for [Sullivan] because he gained the respect of everybody," Richter said. "And then when the season started, it was no question of 'does he deserve to start?' Of course he deserves to start. He can be a difference maker for us at this level."

Even then, Sullivan's emergence was a bit of a slow burn. He had no goal contributions in his first four matches post-break, but a goal and assist against Necaxa in the Leagues Cup got him going, and there have been no shortage of highlight-reel moments since, for both club and country. These included an audacious back-heel for a goal against San Diego FC that showed jaw-dropping levels of skill and improvisation. Those traits were on display for the United States team against Mexico, when he stole an errant pass from El Tri keeper Raúl Rangel and lobbed him from 35 yards.

Even if Sullivan's campaign has been a few notches below MVP caliber, it has still been a season to savor, and a new face excelling in the league is always compelling. There's also the fact that MLS and the Union won't have Sullivan for much longer; he's slated to join Manchester City in January 2028, shortly after his 18th birthday. With the league calendar changing, all that's left of Sullivan's time in MLS is the 2027 sprint season and the first half of the 2027-28 campaign.

The impulse, then, is to enjoy Sullivan's presence in the league -- and shower him with praise -- for as long as it lasts. And who knows what the next 15 months will bring? This year's MLS Young Player of the Year award seems well within reach, but any future success is predicated on making the most of the present. With the postseason approaching, that is the challenge facing Sullivan and the Union coaching staff.

"This game changes so quick. If you look where the last five months have taken him, where's five months from now?" Richter said about Sullivan. "We have to continue to push every single day, focus on getting better.

"A lot can change in a few months, so let's make that a positive change. Every week that goes by, let's make it a positive. Let's make another step forward. That's my responsibility as his coach, is to continue to help him taking steps forward. I know he has a mentality that he'll continue to push to do that."

If Sullivan does that, then trophies of all sorts should come his way.

stories.headline: Lens fans banned from Liverpool match for throwing flares vs. Brugge
stories.summary: Fans of Ligue 1 club Lens were banned from buying tickets for a Champions League game at Liverpool by a UEFA disciplinary ruling Tuesday.
stories.body:
NYON, Switzerland -- Fans of Ligue 1 club Lens were banned from buying tickets for a Champions League game at Liverpool by a UEFA disciplinary ruling on Tuesday.

Lens fans lit dozens of flares and threw some toward rival supporters and the field, forcing the team's Champions League game at Club Brugge last week to be stopped briefly. Lens lost 3-0.

The club already were on probation by UEFA for fans lighting flares and fireworks at a previous Champions League game at Slavia Prague in September.

UEFA said its appeals judges imposed a ban on Lens selling tickets to fans for two Champions League away games.

The sanction will be served when Lens play at Leipzig on Nov. 24 and at Liverpool at Anfield on Jan. 27. A third game ban is deferred for a two-year probationary period.

UEFA said Lens were fined €80,000 ($89,000) for charges of "lighting and throwing of pyrotechnics as well as for acts of damage."

stories.headline: 'It's done': Walker certain to part ways with Roosters
stories.summary: Four-time premiership-winning coach Trent Robinson has declared there's no way back to the Sydney Roosters beyond 2027 for star halfback Sam Walker.
stories.body:
Trent Robinson has ended the Sam Walker contract saga once and for all, insisting there is no way the premiership-winning halfback will play for the Sydney Roosters beyond 2027.

While claiming Walker would remain with the Roosters next season, Robinson on Friday night said the club and hard-nosed chairman Nick Politis were certain to then move the 24-year-old on.

"Nick was pretty clear. We were pretty clear in those negotiations. We knew what we wanted and, no, that's it. It's done there," the Roosters coach told Channel Seven during World Cup commentary.

"Sam's moved on and we've moved on, so there's no way to get a deal done after this."

The Roosters dramatically pulled a contract offer, reportedly worth $1.1 million a season, for Walker to remain at Bondi Junction until at least 2030.

It is understood the Queensland State of Origin playmaker and new Kangaroos debutant was seeking another $200,000 a season.

But, as in negotiations with Latrell Mitchell six years ago, billionaire Politis would not budge.

"No one's done anything wrong. No one's a bad person in this," Robinson said.

"He didn't want to sign. We wanted to sign him for an amount and we couldn't get it done."

The four-time premiership-winning coach maintained Walker had ample time to consider his options.

"Don't forget we started middle of the year in negotiations," Robinson said.

"They pushed it back to after the season, and (now) we're after the season and November 1's coming, and Sam was our biggest contract.

"So therefore a lot of dominoes have to fall after that and other players need to know as well.

"So it was pretty clear in the timeline that we gave him and, I've said before, these deals aren't difficult.

"We're not talking about is this the right club? Am I going to develop in this club as a young player? It's do I want to be here, and is the money right?

"And we couldn't get it done."

Regardless of whether or not Walker is truly part of the Roosters' plans for next season, he will be among the hottest free agents when the NRL trade period opens on Sunday.

With North Queensland and Walker's Maroons and Kangaroos teammate Tom Deardon on Friday saying there was "zero chance" of a swap deal with the Roosters, the premiers are seemingly set to show faith in young gun Toby Rodwell to partner Hugo Savala in the halves after Walker's exit.
